learn.b: The print() function shows text on the screen. Text must go inside quotes, either single or double. Python runs your lines from top to bottom, one at a time.
You can give print() several values separated by commas. Python puts a space between them. You can change that with sep, and change the ending with end.
learn.code:
print('a', 'b', 'c')
print('a', 'b', sep='-')
print('Hi', end='!')
print('there')

learn.b: Inside a string, a backslash starts a special character. \n makes a new line and \t makes a tab. To print a quote inside the same kind of quote, put a backslash before it.
A line that starts with # is a comment. Python ignores it, so you can leave notes for humans. Use comments to explain why your code does something.
learn.code:
# This line is ignored
print('Visible')  # this part is ignored too

learn.b: A variable is a name that points to a value. You create one with =. The value goes on the right and the name goes on the left. Then you can use the name anywhere.

Names can use letters, digits and underscores, but cannot start with a digit or contain spaces. Names are case sensitive, so score and Score are different. Use clear lowercase names like player_score.

learn.b: You can give a variable a new value any time. The right side is worked out first, so x = x + 1 means take x, add 1, and store it back in x.

Every value has a type: int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text, bool for True or False. The type() function tells you which. To swap two variables, use a temporary variable, or write a, b = b, a.

learn.b: Python can do math with + - * and /. The / operator always gives a float, even when the answer is whole. Use ** for powers.
// divides and throws away the decimal part. % gives the remainder. Together they split a number, like turning 125 minutes into 2 hours and 5 minutes. A number is even when n % 2 equals 0.
Python follows the same order as math: parentheses first, then **, then * / // %, then + and -. Use parentheses when you want to be clear.
int() turns a value into a whole number by cutting off decimals, and float() makes a decimal. round(x, n) rounds to n decimal places. abs() gives the positive version of a number.

learn.b: A string is text inside quotes. You can join strings with + and repeat them with *. You can only join a string to another string, so use str() to turn a number into text first.

learn.b: len() counts the characters. Each character has an index starting at 0. Use square brackets to get one character. A negative index counts from the end, so -1 is the last character.
A slice s[start:stop] takes characters from start up to but NOT including stop. If you leave one out, Python goes to the edge. A third number is the step.
Strings are immutable, which means you cannot change one letter in place. To change a string you build a new one. Use triple quotes for text on many lines.
learn.code:
s = 'cat'
# s[0] = 'b'  <- Error
s = 'b' + s[1:]
print(s)

To do math on typed numbers, convert them. int() makes a whole number and float() makes a decimal. Without conversion, '4' + '4' is '44', not 8.

learn.b: The bool type has only two values: True and False. They start with a capital letter. Comparisons produce booleans, so you can print them or store them in variables.
== checks equal, != checks not equal, and < > <= >= compare size. Remember that a single = stores a value, but a double == asks a question. Strings can be compared too.
and is True only if both sides are True. or is True if at least one side is True. not flips a boolean. not goes first, then and, then or.
learn.code:
age = 15
print(age > 10 and age < 20)
print(age < 10 or age > 12)
print(not True)

learn.code:

learn.b: An if statement runs code only when its condition is True. The line ends with a colon, and the code inside is indented by 4 spaces. If the condition is False, Python skips the block.
else gives a backup plan. Its block runs when the if condition is False. Exactly one of the two blocks will run.
Use elif (short for else if) to test more conditions. Python checks from top to bottom and runs only the FIRST block whose condition is True. else at the end catches everything left over.
You can use and, or and not inside a condition, and you can put an if inside another if. Indentation shows which lines belong to which block, so keep it neat.

learn.b: A while loop repeats its block as long as the condition is True. Python checks the condition before every round. When it becomes False, the loop ends.
learn.code:
i = 1
while i <= 3:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1

learn.b: Most while loops need three things: a starting value, a condition, and a change inside the loop. You can write i += 1 as a short way to say i = i + 1. Forget the change and the loop never ends.
learn.code:
total = 0
i = 1
while i <= 4:
    total += i
    i += 1
print(total)

learn.b: If the condition never becomes False, the loop runs forever. That is called an infinite loop. Sometimes it is on purpose: while True runs forever until you use break.
break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of this round and jumps back to the condition check. Use them to handle special cases.

qs.q: What stops a while loop?

qs.why: i goes 1, 2, 3 and the loop stops at 4; each number is on its own line.

learn.b: A for loop goes through a sequence of values, one at a time. range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, so it stops BEFORE the number you give. The loop variable takes each value in turn.
range(start, stop) begins at start and stops before stop. A third number is the step. A negative step counts down.
You can loop directly over a string or a list. The loop variable gets each letter or each item. This is often cleaner than using indexes.
To add things up, make a total before the loop and add to it inside. A loop inside another loop is a nested loop and the inner one runs fully for every round of the outer one.

learn.b: A list holds many values in order, inside square brackets separated by commas. It can hold any types, even mixed. Each item has an index starting at 0.
Lists are mutable: you can change an item by assigning to its index. A negative index counts from the end, so -1 is the last item. Using an index that does not exist causes an error.
len() tells you how many items there are. The in operator checks whether a value is in the list and gives True or False.

learn.b: append(x) adds one item at the end. insert(i, x) adds at index i. extend(other) adds all items of another list. These change the list itself.
remove(x) deletes the first item equal to x. pop() removes and returns the last item, and pop(i) removes the one at index i. del nums[i] also deletes by index.
learn.code:
nums = [5, 6, 7, 8]
nums.remove(6)

learn.b: sort() sorts the list in place and returns None, so do not write x = x.sort(). sort(reverse=True) goes big to small. sorted(x) gives a new sorted list and leaves x alone. reverse() flips the list.

A list slice works like a string slice: nums[1:3] takes indexes 1 and 2. nums[:2] is the first two and nums[-2:] is the last two. sum, min and max work on number lists, and count(x) and index(x) search.
learn.code:
nums = [4, 9, 1, 7]
print(nums[1:3])
print(nums[-2:])
print(sum(nums), min(nums), max(nums))

learn.b: A function is a named block of code you can reuse. You create it with def, a name, parentheses and a colon. The code inside is indented. Nothing happens until you call the function by name.
Parameters are names in the parentheses that receive values when the function is called. The values you pass in are called arguments. The order matters.
return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. print only shows something. If a function has no return, it gives back None. Use return when you want to reuse the result.
learn.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(2, 3)
print(total * 2)

learn.b: A function can return a boolean or choose between results with if. After return runs, nothing else in the function runs. You can also call one function from inside another.
